Mildew
MIL-doo
noun
From the Saxon mele-deaw, honey-dew — the clammy blight that settles on the ear and turns it pale; the Hebrew yeraqon is named from its sickly green-yellow colour, the paleness of a wasting thing.

Biblical Definition

Mildew is the pale blight that settles upon standing grain and rots it where it stands, so that the ear looks fair and yields nothing. Hebrew names it by its colour, yeraqon, the yellow-green pallor of decay; and Scripture never separates it from its twin, blasting. The two go together in every place they appear, and every place is covenantal. They stand in the list of curses God swore against a disobedient Israel (Deu 28:22). They stand in Solomon’s dedicatory prayer, where the king asks that when blasting and mildew come, and a man knows the plague of his own heart and spreads forth his hands toward the house, God in heaven would hear and forgive (1Ki 8:37). They stand in Amos, where God claims them as His stroke and mourns the stubbornness that survived it: “yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amo 4:9). And they stand in Haggai, upon a people who had leisure for their own ceiled houses and none for the LORD’s ruined temple: “I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me” (Hag 2:17). Mildew, then, teaches a hard mercy. God can leave a field standing and still take the bread out of it. He needs no army to humble a nation; a discolouring on the ear will do.

Webster 1828 Definition

A pale blight upon growing grain; with blasting, one of the paired covenant judgments God sends upon the harvest to bring a people to repentance.

MILDEW, a spot or blight upon plants and grain, arising from a clammy dew or damp; it turns the ear pale and spoils the increase.

From the Saxon mele-deaw, honey-dew, the sweet clammy moisture on which the blight was thought to breed.

Hebrew yeraqon, from a root for green or yellow paleness — the colour of a wasting body or a blighted ear.

Named always with blasting: Deu 28:22; 1Ki 8:37; 2Ch 6:28; Amo 4:9; Hag 2:17.

The same Hebrew word is used of the paleness of men’s faces in terror (Jer 30:6).

Key Scripture

Deu 28:22 — "The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish."

1Ki 8:37 — "If there be in the land famine, if there be pestilence, blasting, mildew, locust, or if there be caterpiller; if their enemy besiege them in the land of their cities; whatsoever plague, whatsoever sickness there be;"

Amo 4:9 — "I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD."

Hag 2:17 — "I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye turned not to me, saith the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Chastening is read as bad luck. A blighted field is filed under misfortune, and the summons in it — the call to examine the heart and return — is never heard.

expand to see more

The live misuse of this word is not a redefinition of the fungus but a refusal of the doctrine. Scripture teaches that God governs the increase of the ground and withholds it deliberately; the modern instinct, even among churchgoers, is to sort every loss into accident and every gain into achievement, so that nothing that happens to a man is ever addressed to him. Solomon assumed the opposite. His prayer at the dedication takes it for granted that when mildew comes, the right response is a man knowing “the plague of his own heart” and spreading forth his hands toward the house of God. That is not superstition; it is covenant literacy. Nor does it license the cruelty of reading every man’s hardship as the wages of his particular sin — Job’s friends did that and were rebuked, and our Lord forbade it plainly of the Galileans and of the men of Siloam. The point is not that suffering decodes a private verdict; it is that suffering is not mute. It says: return. And the Lord who forbade the friends’ arithmetic gave the same word Himself — except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fatherly design of chastening. “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth” (Heb 12:6), and the rod on the field is of a piece with the rod on the soul. Mildew took nothing from Israel that God was not willing to restore the moment she turned; the whole tragedy of Amo 4 is the fivefold refrain of a God who kept knocking and a people who kept not answering. Read that chapter and count the strokes — cleanness of teeth, withheld rain, blasting and mildew, pestilence, overthrow — each followed by the same grieved sentence. Then read the end of it: “prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.” The mercy in a blighted harvest is that it comes before that meeting and not after. It is a summons issued while there is still time to answer, and the believer who learns to hear the summons in small losses will not need the large ones.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The pale blight on the ear; with blasting, the covenant stroke that leaves the field standing and takes the bread out of it.

expand to see more

Mildew — Saxon mele-deaw, honey-dew; the clammy blight on grain.

Hebrew yeraqon, paleness, the sickly green-yellow of decay.

Occurs five times, always paired with shiddaphon, blasting.

1Ki 8:37 and 2Ch 6:28 set it in Solomon’s prayer as an occasion for repentance and pardon.

Amo 4:9 and Hag 2:17 make God the express Agent: I have smitten, I smote.

Usage

"Mildew leaves the field standing and empties it — God can humble a nation without an army."

"Solomon’s prayer treats mildew as the occasion for a man to know the plague of his own heart."

"Chastening is never mute; it says return, and it comes before the meeting, not after."
